title: Data Structures and STL Mapping
relevance: Interviewers and OAs probe whether you map abstract structures to the right C++ STL container, quote Big-O correctly (including amortised vs worst-case), and justify the choice under cache, ordering, and iterator constraints.

phases.goal: Map abstract structures to STL types and recall the Big-O that interviews actually ask about.

must_hit.point: Python list/dict/set broadly map to C++ std::vector, std::unordered_map, and std::unordered_set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the three Python↔STL pairs without swapping ordered vs unordered.

must_hit.point: std::vector is the default sequence: index access O(1), end insert/delete amortised O(1), middle insert/delete O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives all three costs and names vector as the default reach-for container.

must_hit.point: Contiguous containers (vector/array/string; deque in blocks) store adjacent elements; node-based ones (list/forward_list/set/map/unordered_*) allocate per-element heap nodes linked by pointers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts contiguous vs node-based and names representative types on each side.

must_hit.point: std::set/map (balanced BST) search/insert/delete are O(log n) with sorted iteration; unordered_set/map are average O(1) and worst-case O(n) on severe collisions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates tree O(log n)+order from hash average O(1)/worst O(n)+no order.

must_hit.point: std::priority_queue is a binary heap (default max-heap on vector): push/pop O(log n), top O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States default max-heap, underlying vector, and the three operation costs.

probes: What is the complexity of vector::push_back?
Map each of dynamic array, hash table, and balanced BST to its STL type and the Big-O of the operations that matter.

hints.1: Start from the abstract structure, then name the STL type before quoting costs.
hints.2: For push_back, separate amortised end growth from a single reallocation spike.
hints.3: Say amortised O(1), worst-case O(n) on reallocation; vector=[]; unordered_map/set=hash; set/map=tree O(log n).

phases.goal: Show the signatures and behavioral rules that change correctness: invalidation, adaptor APIs, map lookup, heap/list quirks.

must_hit.point: vector push_back/insert/reserve that reallocates invalidates all iterators, references, and pointers; erase invalidates at/after the erase point.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions full invalidation on growth and partial invalidation on erase; suggests holding indices or re-getting iterators.

must_hit.point: stack/queue/priority_queue pop() returns void — read with top()/front() first, then pop().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the void return and the two-step read-then-pop pattern across adaptors.

must_hit.point: map::operator[] default-inserts a missing key; pure queries should use find, at, or contains (C++20); at throws if absent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that [] mutates the map on miss and names the read-only alternatives.

must_hit.point: Min-heap priority_queue needs the three-argument form with std::vector and std::greater; default less yields largest on top.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>> and contrasts with the default max-heap.

must_hit.point: forward_list has no size() or push_back; insert_after/erase_after need the iterator before the victim (use before_begin() to insert at front).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the missing APIs and the before-iterator / before_begin pattern.

probes: How do you get a min-heap from std::priority_queue?
What happens to iterators when a vector grows, and how do you safely look up in a map without inserting?

hints.1: Think about what the adaptor does not return and what map[] does on a miss.
hints.2: Contrast growth invalidation on vector with read-only map lookup APIs.
hints.3: top()/front() then pop(); map find/at/contains; min-heap = vector + greater; forward_list uses insert_after/before_begin.

phases.goal: Explain when Big-O misleads and how order, worst-case, and cache locality drive the real choice.

must_hit.point: Amortised O(1) (e.g. vector::push_back, end ops on deque/string) averages O(1) over a long sequence but a single call may be O(n) on reallocation; map insert O(log n) and list splice O(1) are true worst-case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines amortised vs guaranteed worst-case and names examples of each.

must_hit.point: Do not pick std::list only because insert is O(1): without a pre-held iterator, finding the spot is still O(n), same asymptotic as vector::insert but with worse constants and locality.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Requires the iterator precondition and compares find+splice cost to vector middle insert.

must_hit.point: Prefer vector unless you need stable iterators under middle insert/erase and already hold the iterator (splice-heavy / LRU-style); contiguous memmove often beats pointer-chasing list nodes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States vector-default with the narrow list exceptions tied to held iterators and locality.

must_hit.point: Choose unordered_map/set for average O(1) when order does not matter; choose map/set for sorted iteration, lower_bound, or hard O(log n) worst-case against adversarial keys.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames the decision as order-needed? and worst-case-needed? with the matching container.

probes: When would you use std::list over std::vector?
map vs unordered_map — what do you optimize for?

hints.1: Ask whether you already hold an iterator and whether you need sorted order or hard latency.
hints.2: Separate Big-O operation counts from wall-clock/cache behavior and amortised spikes.
hints.3: list only with held iterator/splice/stability; unordered for average speed; map for order or O(log n) worst-case; pre-reserve or true worst-case structures when amortised spikes hurt.

phases.goal: Pick a container from requirements and know how to build structures the STL does not ship.

must_hit.point: Decision axes: need sorted/insertion/no order? duplicates? random index? insert at end / both ends / middle with iterator? worst-case vs amortised? cache locality? Unsure → vector.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the axes in order and defaults to vector when nothing forces another type.

must_hit.point: Typical picks: append+index → vector; sliding window push back/pop front → deque (or queue if no index); sorted predecessor → map/set; word frequencies → unordered_map; highest priority → priority_queue; undo → stack; fixed-width flags → bitset; O(1) erase of a known LRU node → list plus map to iterators.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps several concrete requirements to one STL type each without inventing extras.

must_hit.point: C++ has no built-in graph: represent with an adjacency list such as vector<vector<int>> (or unordered_map to vector for non-int IDs).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States no graph container and gives the adjacency-list construction.

must_hit.point: Prefer std::bitset<N> (or manual vector of uint64_t) over vector<bool>; deque is not contiguous so do not pass &dq[0] to a C API expecting one block—use vector::data().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects vector<bool> for bit packs and rejects deque for contiguous C buffers.

probes: Which container and why for a sliding window that needs push back, pop front, and occasional indexing?
How would you represent a graph in C++?
Why might deque be wrong for a C-style buffer API?

hints.1: Name the requirement that rules containers out before naming the winner.
hints.2: Both-ends growth plus indexing points to deque; contiguous C APIs point to vector.
hints.3: Sliding window with index → deque; graph → vector of vectors adjacency list; C buffer → vector::data(), not deque.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: vector middle insert is O(n) element moves but tight contiguous memmove and great locality; list insert/erase is O(1) only with a held iterator, finding the position is O(n), and each node is a separate allocation. Prefer vector unless you need stable middle iterators, splice, or already hold the position.

vector::push_back and end ops on deque/string are amortised O(1) but may spike to O(n) on reallocation; map insert O(log n) and list splice O(1) never surprise with a linear spike. For hard real-time, prefer true worst-case bounds or pre-reserve.

unordered_* win on average O(1) when order is irrelevant but risk worst-case O(n) under collisions and need hashable keys; map/set give guaranteed O(log n), sorted iteration, and lower_bound/range queries.

Prefer vector if you only grow at the back (cache-friendly, contiguous, data() for C APIs). Prefer deque when you need fast push/pop at both ends plus occasional O(1) indexing; deque is not guaranteed contiguous.
For fixed-width bit algebra use bitset<N>; for runtime-sized packs prefer vector of uint64_t. Avoid vector<bool>—it is a specialisation with proxy references and nonstandard container semantics.

gotchas.trap: Answering that vector::push_back is simply O(1).
gotchas.correction: It is amortised O(1); worst-case O(n) on reallocation. Say which bound you mean.

gotchas.trap: Choosing std::list because middle insert is O(1).
gotchas.correction: O(1) only if you already hold an iterator to the splice point; otherwise finding the spot is O(n), usually slower than vector in practice.

gotchas.trap: Calling pop() on stack/queue/priority_queue expecting the removed value.
gotchas.correction: pop() returns void; call top() or front() first, then pop().

gotchas.trap: Using map::operator[] for a read-only lookup.
gotchas.correction: [] default-inserts if the key is missing; use find, at, or contains for pure queries.

gotchas.trap: Assuming priority_queue is a min-heap / supports decrease-key.
gotchas.correction: Default is max-heap (less); min-heap needs vector + greater. No iterators, no erase-by-value, no true decrease-key—use lazy deletion or a custom heap.

gotchas.trap: Passing &dq[0] (or assuming deque is one contiguous block) to a C API.
gotchas.correction: deque is not guaranteed contiguous; use vector and data().

gotchas.trap: Comparing string::find's result to -1 as a signed int.
gotchas.correction: On failure find returns string::npos; compare against npos.

gotchas.trap: Treating std::array like a dynamic container or mixing different N as the same type.
gotchas.correction: N is part of the type; no push_back; array<int,5> and array<int,6> are different types.

gotchas.trap: Expecting forward_list::size or list-style insert at an iterator to the victim.
gotchas.correction: No size()/push_back; insert_after/erase_after take the iterator before the position; use before_begin() for the front.
